photos.desc: Tree roots have deformed the sidewalk.
The sidewalk has cracks and asphalt patching, apparently also pushed up by tree roots.
The sidewalk has some cracks and is uneven.
Tree roots have heaved the sidewalk.
Tree roots have heaved the sidewalk.
Hard to see clearly, but the sidewalk seems very narrow and somewhat damaged.
Different paving materials, with some level differences.
The sidewalk is uneven, apparently also pushed up by tree roots.
The sidewalk is uneven, with an obvious level difference.
Same spot as R248 (two photos of the same location); the level difference is quite obvious.
The sidewalk on the left appears to have a slight level difference.
There are cracks in the sidewalk.
The sidewalk has cracks and a level difference.
The sidewalk is under construction and suddenly changes from concrete to asphalt.
The sidewalk looks discontinuous, with some cracks in the middle.
The sidewalk has obvious cracks, apparently pushed apart by a tree.
The sidewalk has been lifted by tree roots, creating a level difference.
The sidewalk is relatively damaged, and there seems to be a drop because of the driveway.
The sidewalk is damaged.
The sidewalk is taken up by garbage bins.
The sidewalk is taken up by garbage bins, traffic cones and other clutter.
The sidewalk has cracks and level differences.
The sidewalk has been lifted by a tree, creating a level difference.
Garbage bins are placed along the sidewalk.
The sidewalk is blocked by garbage bins.
Garbage bins are not placed against the edge and slightly block the path.
The sidewalk is interrupted: to reach the next intersection, pedestrians must first cross a parking-lot exit and then walk a stretch with no sidewalk.
A vendor's stall on the sidewalk makes the walkway very narrow.
Curb ramp has no tactile paving (detectable warning).
The sidewalk is almost completely occupied; pedestrians must go around to walk under the scaffolding inside. (On a second visit the sidewalk was already passable.)
Sidewalk is fenced off; pedestrians must turn a corner to enter a temporary sidewalk.
One section of the pavement is cracked and patched; the sidewalk around it appears to be flat. Two photos of the same spot.

Sidewalk is closed with end-detour signs; the temporary asphalt acts as an improvised curb cut with no consideration of slope. A teammate recalled there was no curb cut here. May be temporary. Two photos of the same spot.
Curb ramp has some grooves but nothing comparable to standard tactile paving; the ramp flares outward instead of being recessed, so a wheelchair user faces a steep drop.
No curb cut at all; a wheelchair user cannot get down from the sidewalk.
Sidewalk is narrow, making it hard for a wheelchair user to pass; cracked slab around a utility vault cover.
A single traffic cone stands in the middle of the sidewalk, marking a hole (open utility box) beneath it.
White van parked directly on the sidewalk, taking over pedestrian space even though some room is left to pass.
Pedestrians must go around via the curb ramp in the roadway to reach the sidewalk on the other side.
Sidewalk is interrupted (same situation as P28); pedestrians must step into the temporary roadway to continue.
No actual sidewalk (likely construction); pedestrians must walk out into the street and detour back onto the sidewalk. May be temporary.
Sidewalk is interrupted by construction, but an alternative sidewalk next to it can be used. May be temporary.
Construction fencing blocks the corner; unclear whether a route continues, but pedestrians must detour around the whole block. May be temporary.
The middle of the sidewalk is full of obstacles (traffic cones, dirt/excavated soil); pedestrians can barely get through.
The original sidewalk is completely unusable; only a temporary alternative walkway can be used. May be temporary.
A curb cut suddenly appears in the sidewalk and is poorly designed; no tactile paving.
A box on the sidewalk clearly blocks people from passing.
No tactile paving; the ground approaching the ramp is broken up, with steel plates and utility boxes.
The only curb cut at this corner is non-standard and does not connect to the crosswalk; a wheelchair user must first go down into the roadway and then turn back toward the sidewalk.
Sidewalk is discontinuous: it ends partway and turns into a park/grass lot.
Curb ramp is relatively steep and has no yellow tactile (truncated dome) paving, so it is unfriendly to blind and low-vision pedestrians.
Freeway exit with a channelizing island lets drivers turn at speed; several drivers did not notice the pedestrian.
Belongings and a tarp block the sidewalk; it is impossible to pass without walking down into the street.
An uncovered round hole, recessed and filled with leaves, sits in the walking surface and could catch a cane or small wheel.
An uncovered, recessed round hole filled with leaves sits within the slab and could catch a cane tip or small wheel.
Slabs are split by wide open cracks with missing pieces and uneven edges, creating trip and wheel hazards.
Large sections of pavement are missing and filled with weeds along the curbside part of the walkway.
Construction fencing closes the corner, pushing pedestrians onto temporary asphalt between the fence and orange barriers.
Temporary plywood covers much of the width, with gaps and uneven edges; a narrower concrete strip remains beside the wall.
Temporary plywood leaves a raised, splintered edge and gap; only the narrower concrete strip beside it stays even.
The curbside half has many offset broken slabs, open cracks, and crumbled patches; the other half is smoother.
Missing chunks, shallow holes, and broken edges on both sides leave only a narrow intact strip in the middle.
A ragged, broken ledge along one slab joint creates a small level difference across part of the path.
The curb drops to a grooved apron at the crossing with no tactile domes to warn low-vision pedestrians.
Box stacks and a wire rack on the sidewalk pinch the path ahead into a tight gap for wheelchairs or strollers.
Stacked produce boxes, stands, and a stool leave a narrow opening, which a person is partly occupying in this view.
A broken utility lid leaves open holes in mid-sidewalk, partly covered by an overturned cone base.
Across the street, fencing and barriers meet the roadway, with no open pedestrian walkway visible along that side.
A wide grass-filled joint has an exposed slab edge indicating a level difference that could catch wheels or canes.
Grass fills irregular missing sections of pavement, and a broken longitudinal crack with open edges runs through the foreground.
The crosswalk approaches a corner with raised red curb; no aligned curb ramp or tactile paving is visible at the landing.
A jagged break crosses the sidewalk, with a visible lip, small gap, and further broken paving near the wall.
Two jagged holes with broken concrete sit in a curbside slab and could catch canes or wheels; clear width remains.
Grass and dirt replace pavement along the curb; paved sidewalk appears only farther ahead, leaving no firm route here.
Raised red curb wraps the corner without tactile paving; cracked, offset gutter slabs surround the drain at the crossing approach.
Ahead beside the tree, a broken slab is tilted up with a clear raised edge; the near pavement is flat.
Broken slabs beside the tree are lifted and offset, forming distinct lips and open cracks in the walking path.
A large recessed cutout filled with leaves and weeds interrupts the pavement, creating a wheel, cane, and trip hazard.
The sidewalk ends in broken pavement and loose gravel beside a raised slab edge, a rough improvised transition to the crosswalk.
A red pickup farther ahead stands on the sidewalk and takes up much of its curbside width.
A pickup parked on the sidewalk takes up much of its width ahead; a narrower gap remains beside the buildings.
A large red utility truck is parked on the sidewalk, taking much of the width and narrowing passage beside the building.
A large tarp-covered pile spans the pavement from the planting area to the curb, leaving no visible way past.
A crumbling utility cover has a missing side piece filled with debris, beside cracked, weedy slab joints.
Foreground panels have broken edges, open gaps, and slightly uneven joints along the walking line.
A round cover in the walkway has a broken rim and partial opening that could catch a cane or small wheel.
Taped cones and plywood occupy both sides of the sidewalk, squeezing pedestrians through a narrower middle gap.
Tall exposed anchor bolts and a pipe protrude from a temporary asphalt patch with loose gravel on the corner sidewalk.
A rough temporary asphalt wedge serves as an improvised curb ramp, with abrupt edges and no tactile paving.
A fence diverts walkers off the curb onto a makeshift plywood platform between barriers, with edge gaps and no tactile warning.
Temporary plywood covers the middle of the sidewalk; its near edge is raised over an open gap, a trip and wheel hazard.
Construction fencing occupies the corner; only roadway asphalt between fence and barriers remains beside the pedestrian push button.
Fencing closes off the corner, leaving a narrowing passage on roadway asphalt with bicycle markings between fence and water barriers.
Construction fence and water barriers frame a passage on roadway asphalt; the nearest visible sidewalk lies across the pavement beyond.
Water barriers and a Sidewalk Closed sign block the sidewalk ahead, so pedestrians cannot continue along it.
A utility lid on the corner approach is cracked with a broken, open corner, which could catch a cane or small wheel.
Jagged concrete edges meet a dark asphalt patch beside the wall with a visible lip; clear sidewalk remains to the left.
Produce stands, crates, carts, and cardboard line both sides and take up much of the sidewalk, constraining the route ahead.
Produce tables, crates, and boxes on both sides take up much of the sidewalk, leaving a constricted shared aisle.
A partly framed utility cover in the walkway is broken, with missing pieces, small openings, and uneven edges.
A crumbled, cracked patch meets the next slab at a ragged uneven edge across the fence side of the walk.
A pallet, mattress, overflowing bin, and loose wood occupy about half the sidewalk, narrowing the route toward the corner.
Next to large tree roots, a raised cracked edge runs across the sidewalk from the tree well toward the wall.
The fully visible corner ramp has grooves but no tactile domes, giving low-vision pedestrians a weaker cue at the street edge.
A white pickup stands across the driveway crossing, blocking much of the sidewalk line and forcing a detour toward the street.
A fence closes off the tarp-covered corner, diverting pedestrians to an asphalt strip between the fence and traffic barriers.
A low, spreading tree and cardboard boxes occupy much of the sidewalk, leaving a narrow passage beside the fence.
